title: Commentariorum In Micheam Prophetam Libri Duo
author: Jerome
source: Translated by Claude from tmp474.tmp474.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: (Vers. 9, 10.) « Mulieres populi mei ejecistis de domo deliciarum suarum : a parvulis earum tu- listis laudem meam in perpetuum. Surgite et ite, quia non habetis hic requiem, propter immundi- tiam suam [Vulg. ejus] corrumpetur putredine pessima. » Interpretatio Septuaginta (si tamen Septuaginta est; Josephus enim scribit, et Hebraei tradunt, quinque tantum libros legis Moysi ab eis translatos, et Ptolemaeo regi traditos [Al. contra- ditos]) tantum discordat in praesenti loco ab He- braica veritate, ut nec capita possimus ex aequo ponere, nec eorum simul sententias explicare.
passages.english: (Verses 9, 10.) "You have cast the women of my people out of the house of their delights; from their little ones you have taken away my praise for ever. Arise and go, for you have no rest here; because of its uncleanness it will be corrupted with a most grievous rottenness." The rendering of the Seventy (if indeed it is the Seventy; for Josephus writes, and the Hebrews hand down, that only the five books of the law of Moses were translated by them and delivered to King Ptolemy) differs so greatly in the present passage from the Hebrew truth that we can neither set out the headings side by side nor explain their meanings together.
passages.notes: "suam [Vulg. ejus]" and "traditos [Al. contraditos]" are editorial variant notes; the variants do not change the sense. "Capita" ("headings") likely means the individual clauses or sections of the text.

passages.original: Semper invidis respondemus, quia non cessat invidia, et librorum nostrorum exordia, aemu- lorum maledicta confutant : qui vulgo jactant, me sterilis jejunique sermonis quasdam ineptias scri- bere, et cum loqui nesciam, tacere non posse. Itaque obsecro vos, o Paula et Eustochium, ut ad hujuscemodi latratus claudatis aures, et infan- tiam, ut dicunt, meam orationibus adjurantes, impetretis mihi juxta Apostolum adapertionem oris mei, ut de Scripturis loquenti adaptari possit : Dominus dabit verbum evangelizantibus virtute multa (Psal.LXVII, 12). Moneo autem tauros pin- gues, qui circumdederunt me (Psal.XXI), ut quie- scant et desinant maledicere, malefacta ne noscant sua, quae proferentur post, si pergent [Al. per- gunt] laedere. Nam quod dicunt, Origenis me vo- lumina compilare, et contaminari non decere ve- terum scripta : quod illi maledictum vehemens esse existimant 1, eamdem laudem ego maximam duco, cum illum imitari volo, quem cunctis pru- dentibus et vobis placere non dubito.
passages.english: We are always answering the envious, because envy does not cease, and the opening of our books refutes the abuse of our rivals, who boast publicly that I write certain absurdities in a barren and starved style, and that although I do not know how to speak, I cannot keep silent. Therefore I beseech you, Paula and Eustochium, to close your ears to barking of this kind, and, aiding my 'infancy' (as they call it) with your prayers, to obtain for me, according to the Apostle, the opening of my mouth, so that this may be fitted to me as I speak about the Scriptures: "The Lord will give the word to those who preach the gospel with great power" (Ps. 67:12). And I warn the fat bulls that have surrounded me (Ps. 21) to be quiet and stop their abuse, lest they come to know their own misdeeds, which will be brought out afterwards if they go on doing harm. For as to their saying that I plunder the volumes of Origen, and that it is not proper for the writings of the ancients to be contaminated: what they think is a violent reproach, I count as the highest praise, since I wish to imitate him who, I do not doubt, pleases all wise men and you.
passages.notes: "malefacta ne noscant sua, quae proferentur post, si pergent laedere" adapts a line from the prologue of Terence's Eunuch. "Contaminari" echoes Terence's term for combining source plays. "Si pergent [Al. pergunt]": the variant does not change the sense. The "1" after "existimant" is a footnote mark and has been omitted.

passages.original: Et disperdentur legitima populi mei, sive Amri, et omnia opera domus Achab, eorum qui in haeresibus patriarchae, et principes exstiterunt. Quos possumus, vel ad contrarias referre virtutes, vel ad haeresiarchas, ut fuit Marcion et Basilides, et nuper Arius, et Eunomius. Et ambulastis in vo- luntatibus eorum, Amri videlicet et Achab. Pul- chreque ait, in voluntatibus eorum. Doctrina enim magistrorum nequam, non est doctrina Dei, sed adinventiones cordis illorum.
passages.english: And the statutes of my people, or of Omri, will be destroyed, and all the works of the house of Ahab, that is, of those who stood out as patriarchs and princes in the heresies. These we can refer either to the opposing powers or to heresiarchs, such as Marcion and Basilides were, and recently Arius and Eunomius. And you have walked in their wills, that is, of Omri and Ahab. And he says well, "in their wills." For the teaching of wicked masters is not the teaching of God, but the inventions of their own heart.
passages.notes: "Legitima" (statutes, ordinances) renders Jerome's version of Micah 6:16. "Contrarias virtutes" is taken as hostile spiritual powers.

passages.original: licet illae ad iracundiam provocent, et talia fa- ciant per quae mereantur amaritudinem sustinere. Hoc enim significat παραπιχραίνεσθα: : tamen vos nolite eis in amaritudine vicem reddere. Sed et Salomon in Ecclesiaste : Et hominem, inquit, unum de mille inveni, et mulierem in his omnibus non inveni (Eccle.VII, 29) : forsitan suo doctus exemplo, mulieribus non credendum, per quas offenderat (??) (III Reg.XI). Sed et poeta sublimis (non numerus alter, ut Lucilius [Al. Lucilius] de Ennio suspicatur; sed primus Homerus apud Latinos). Varium et mutabile semper Femina 519 Plenae sunt historiae Graecae et Latinae, quanti viri ab uxoribus suis decepti sini eorum- que vita sit prodita.
passages.english: even if they provoke [you] to anger and do such things as deserve to suffer bitterness. For this is what *parapikrainesthai* [to be embittered, provoked] means: nevertheless, do not repay them in bitterness. And Solomon too, in Ecclesiastes, says: "One man among a thousand I have found, and a woman among all these I have not found" (Eccl. 7:29); perhaps taught by his own example that women are not to be trusted, through whom he had given offence (1 Kings 11). And also the sublime poet (not a "second Homer", as Lucilius suspects of Ennius, but the first Homer among the Latins): "A fickle and changeable thing always is woman." Greek and Latin histories are full of how many men have been deceived by their wives and had their lives betrayed.
passages.notes: The Greek is garbled in the scan (παραπιχραίνεσθα:), read as παραπικραίνεσθαι. "Non numerus alter" appears corrupt; probably "non Homerus alter" ("not a second Homer"), translated so. The bracketed "[Al. Lucilius]" is an editorial variant note and "(??)" a printed query; both omitted. The quotation is Virgil, Aeneid 4.569–70, and the "sublime poet" is Virgil. "519" is a stray page number and is omitted. "sini" is read as "sint".
